slides.title: Review item 1
slides.html:
Prove that when you add two multiples of 4, you always get a multiple of 4.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

By the definition of a multiple, m=4r and n=4s for integers r, s. Then m+n=4r+4s=4(r+s). Since integers are closed under addition, r+s is an integer, so m+n is a multiple of 4.

Reveal second check

Difference is a parallel independent result: m-n=4(r-s). The sum proof uses only a definition, distributivity and integer closure, not selected numerical cases.

slides.title: Review item 2
slides.html:
Use an indirect proof to show: if the square of an integer is odd, then the integer is odd. Then say which integers have a square of 81.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume n² is odd but n is not odd. Every integer is even or odd, so n=2k for an integer k. Then n²=4 k²=2(2 k²) is even, contradicting the given odd square. Therefore n is odd. For the specified square the possible integers are plus or minus 9, both odd.

Reveal second check

The contrapositive supplies a second route: an even integer 2k has even square 4 k². This is equivalent to the claim. No ruler postulate, triangle theorem or drawing is used.

slides.title: Review item 3
slides.html:
Two segments in a drawing have no marks, but they seem equal in length. Were you given that they are equal? How could you make sure?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. Appearance supplies neither measurement nor a hypothesis. If endpoints are on an explicitly calibrated ruler at 0, 5 and 7, 12, both distances equal 5; otherwise obtain an equality mark, measurement assumption or proof.

Reveal second check

Countermodel: redraw one segment slightly longer while retaining all stated incidence facts. The original assumptions remain true but equality fails.

slides.title: Review item 4
slides.html:
For n = 0, 1, 2 the values are 1, 3, 5. Does this show that f(n) = 2n + 1 works for every whole number n? Compare two rules at n = 6.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. Both f(n)=2n+1 and g(n)=2n+1+n(n-1)(n-2) fit all three data points, but f(6)=13 and g(6)=133. A proof needs a rule or hypothesis controlling every n.

Reveal second check

Direct substitution n=0, 1, 2 makes the extra product zero each time; at n=6 all its factors are positive. This is an exact counterexample to uniqueness.

slides.title: Review item 5
slides.html:
What do two different points determine? How are a line, a ray and a segment different?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Two distinct points determine exactly one line. Segment AB includes its two endpoints and points between them. Ray AB starts at A and extends through B without a second endpoint. The line extends both ways and has infinitely many points.

Reveal second check

A third collinear point lies on the same unique line; two coincident named points do not satisfy the distinctness hypothesis.

slides.title: Review item 6
slides.html:
Model: the Earth is a sphere and sunlight is parallel. Two cities on one north-south circle are 600 km apart along the surface, with a center angle of 6 degrees. Estimate the distance around the Earth.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The arc is 6/360 of a full circle, so C=600·360/6=36000 km. The shadow-angle to central-angle identification is a preview assumption here; its parallel-line proof comes in Unit 5.

Reveal second check

The circumference divided by 360 is 100 km per degree; 6 degrees then gives 600 km, matching the input.

slides.title: Review item 7
slides.html:
A convex polygon has 4 sides. How many vertices and sides does it have, and how many diagonals start at one vertex?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

There are 4 vertices and 4 sides. From one vertex there are 3 other vertices; exclude its two neighbors, leaving 1 diagonal. This is counting, not an early assertion of the angle-sum formula.

Reveal second check

Total diagonal count would be 4(4-3)/2=2, since each diagonal is counted at both ends.

slides.title: Review item 8
slides.html:
Using only a compass and straightedge, copy a length of 5 onto a ray that starts at P. Explain why the copy is 5 long.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Set the compass opening to the given segment. With center P draw an arc crossing the specified ray at Q. Since Q is on that radius-5 circle, PQ=5. The chosen ray fixes the intended forward intersection.

Reveal second check

Circle definition alone supplies the equality; neither a ruler reading nor triangle congruence is needed.

slides.title: Review item 9
slides.html:
In our system, 'incidence' (a point lying on a line) is undefined. What does that mean? Can we assume anything we like about it?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

A formal theory begins with primitive objects/relations and assumptions about them rather than defining every term using other terms. Undefined does not mean unrestricted: axioms constrain allowed models. A theorem is derived from those axioms and definitions.

Reveal second check

Interpret the same incidence axioms in two different labeled diagrams. Renaming points does not change truth; adding an unlicensed incidence can violate an axiom. This separates vocabulary from constraints.

slides.title: Review item 10
slides.html:
n is an integer. Write the contrapositive of 'if n is divisible by 10, then n is divisible by 5.' Then prove the original statement from the definitions.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

If n=10k for an integer k, then n=5(2k), so n is divisible by 5. Contrapositive: if n is not divisible by 5, then n is not divisible by 10.

Reveal second check

The inclusion of integer multiples of 10 among multiples of 5 checks the original; the logical truth table checks equivalence with the contrapositive.

slides.title: Review item 11
slides.html:
Is 'a quadrilateral with at least one right angle' a good definition of a rectangle? If not, write a correct one.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The proposed condition admits a quadrilateral with stipulated angles90,60,120,90degrees, so it is not sufficient. Exact replacement: rectangle if and only if quadrilateral with four right angles. Both necessity and sufficiency are part of the definition.

Reveal second check

Check the replacement in each direction: a named rectangle satisfies the condition by the adopted definition; any object satisfying the full condition is a rectangle. The original counterexample no longer qualifies.

slides.title: Review item 13
slides.html:
Prove indirectly: if an integer's square is odd, the integer is odd. Use it when the square is 49, and check n = 7.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Assume n² is odd but n is not odd. Every integer is even or odd, so n=2k for an integer k. Then n²=4 k²=2(2 k²) is even, contradicting the given odd square. Therefore n is odd. For the specified square the possible integers are plus or minus 7, both odd. n²=49 is odd and n=7 is odd; this check illustrates the proved universal statement, not a replacement for its proof.

Reveal second check

The contrapositive supplies a second route: an even integer 2k has even square 4 k². This is equivalent to the claim. No ruler postulate, triangle theorem or drawing is used.

slides.title: Review item 14
slides.html:
A made-up rule says z = 2x + 1, and you are given x = 4. Which part is the definition, which is the given, and which is the result?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The rule z=2x+1 is the stipulated definition of the operation. x=4 is the given input. Substitution derives z=2·4+1=9; the output 9 is a result, not another assumption.

Reveal second check

Running the inverse calculation(9-1)/2 returns 4. All required rules are printed here; no ruler or midpoint theorem is used.

slides.title: Review item 15
slides.html:
The same segment PQ has two written labels in the same units: PQ = 4 and PQ = 6. The drawing says 'not to scale.' Does that note fix the conflict? Could redrawing the segment make both labels true?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No to both. One length cannot equal two different numbers in the same units. Not to scale permits a schematic picture, not contradictory exact data. One written datum must be corrected or the problem must be declared inconsistent; changing the pixels cannot satisfy both.

Reveal second check

Substituting PQ=4 into PQ=6 would give 4=6, which is false independently of every drawing. Changing display scale does not change either asserted numerical value.

geo.solution: No to both. One length cannot equal two different numbers in the same units. Not to scale permits a schematic picture, not contradictory exact data. One written datum must be corrected or the problem must be declared inconsistent; changing the pixels cannot satisfy both.

slides.title: Review item 16
slides.html:
A designer checks some triangles and other closed paths that don't cross themselves, then guesses: every closed path made of straight segments is a simple polygon. A new card shows the closed path A-B-C-D-A and says that sides AB and CD cross at X, inside both sides. What does this card show? Could more examples that work save the guess?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The card refutes the universal conjecture. Its path is closed and straight-edged, so it meets the hypothesis, but the stated nonconsecutive crossing violates the definition of a simple polygon. More successful examples cannot erase this valid counterexample. A narrower replacement conjecture would require its own justification.

Reveal second check

Write H for closed and straight-edged, and S for simple polygon. The card has H true and S false, exactly the false case for H implies S. The conclusion uses the stipulated crossing, not an apparent crossing inferred from pixels.

slides.title: Common traps
slides.html:
• 1.1: A figure that looks equal is equal.
  • 1.2: Enough examples prove a rule.
  • 1.3: Lines are segments with ends.
  • 1.4: Angle size depends on ray length.
  • 1.5: Any closed figure is a polygon (circles, curved sides).
  • 1.6: The compass is only for circles, not for transferring lengths.
  • 1.7: Every word can be defined.
  • 1.8: The converse of a true statement is true.
  • 1.9: A definition only has to work one way.
  • 1.10: A proof is a list of true facts in any order.
  • 1.11: Indirect proof means proving the opposite is true.
  • 1.12: Theorems and postulates are the same kind of thing.
